description:
SHIPPED s473v (2026-09-16), member 4 of perf round 33.  Runtime-only.

=== THE PROFILE (sb-sprof :cpu, self time, on 2ac855aa) ===
20 000 sorts of 50 elements = 2.6 us per sort against perl's 1.2.

  sortnum (1052 samples)              sortstr (1493 samples)
   26.0 % stable-sort-simple-vector    25.0 % sb-kernel:%sp-string-compare
   24.3 % <   (a FULL call per          22.0 % sb-kernel:string<*
          comparison, ~280 per sort)    16.5 % stable-sort-simple-vector
    4.6 % %map-for-effect-arity-1       14.3 % string<
    3.9 % the `every #'realp' wrapper    2.5 % %p-array-bulk-source
    3.5 % vector-push-extend             1.6 % %map-for-effect-arity-1
    3.2/2.5 % data-vector ref/set        1.3 % %p-sort-collect-plain
    2.3 % %pcl-nan-p                     1.1 % vector-push-extend
    1.8 % %p-sort-collect-plain self
    1.4 % the `notany #'%pcl-nan-p' wrapper

THREE COSTS, and none of them is the sort:
 1. THE PREDICATE.  `#'<` is the generic function: a full call with numeric
    type dispatch, once per comparison.  On sortstr it is worse â CL's
    `string<` parses four keyword arguments, dispatches on the string TYPE and
    answers a mismatch INDEX where a sort wants a boolean: **61.3 % of the
    row** across its three frames.
 2. THE CLASSIFICATION.  `every #'realp` then `notany #'%pcl-nan-p` (or
    `every #'stringp`) are TWO more passes over the values with a funcall per
    element: 13.5 % of sortnum.
 3. THE COLLECTION.  An adjustable vector grown from 16 by vector-push-extend
    (two growths at 50 elements) and then copy-seq'd: %p-sort-collect-plain is
    21.4 % TOTAL on sortnum.

=== THE SHAPE ===
 * %p-sort-plain-vector â the ONE-SOURCE-ARRAY case (`sort @a`, which is what
   every classic sort in a program looks like) knows its length up front and
   collects straight into a right-sized simple-vector: no adjustable vector,
   no growths, no copy-seq.  %p-sort-values picks it; %p-sort-collect-general
   keeps the old walk (%p-sort-collect-plain, unchanged) for many sources and
   scalar sources.
 * %p-sort-kind â ONE typed pass answering (values KIND SAW-NAN) over
   :fixnum / :double / :real / :sstring (all SIMPLE strings) / :string /
   :mixed.  The NaN answer comes from the SAME walk, because a NaN sends the
   whole sort to the generic path (#996, D5) and asking separately was the
   second of the two passes.
 * %p-fix< / %p-fix> / %p-dbl< / %p-dbl> â typed predicates, and
   %p-sstring< / %p-sstring> â a code-point loop over two simple strings,
   which is the order CL's `string<` gives and perl's `cmp` means, as a
   BOOLEAN.
 * %p-sort-numeric / %p-sort-stringly dispatch on the kind; both keep a `t`
   arm that is the DECORATED path â a correct general answer for every kind,
   which is why it is not a rule-12 swallow (the docstring says so).  The MODE
   set, where a wrong guess would be a wrong ORDER, still dies on an unknown
   value (%p-sort-classic-numeric-p, unchanged).

=== THE NUMBERS (A/B, one emission, two cores, interleaved best-of-5) ===
BENCH_RT_B = the 2ac855aa runtime; B/A positive = the OLD runtime is slower.
`uptime` at the end: load 2.64 2.09 2.01.

  bench       perl(s)   pclA(s)   pclB(s)     B/A    A/perl    (was)
  sortstr      0.0744    0.0523    0.1300  +148.7%   0.70x    (1.55x)
  sortnum      0.0271    0.0426    0.0762   +78.6%   1.58x    (2.63x)
  strcat       0.3056    0.3049    0.6846  +124.6%   1.00x    -- #1809's
  arrfill      0.0519    0.0283    0.0314   +11.0%   0.55x    control
  slices       0.0767    0.1279    0.1244    -2.8%   1.67x    control
  listcopy     0.5526    0.2068    0.2098    +1.5%   0.37x    control
  feread       0.5324    0.1379    0.1366    -0.9%   0.26x    control
  feread2      0.5303    0.1401    0.1391    -0.7%   0.26x    control
  feread3      0.5379    0.1376    0.1461    +6.1%   0.26x    control

**PCL IS NOW FASTER THAN PERL ON sortstr** (0.70x, from 1.55x).  arrfill's
+11.0 % and feread3's +6.1 % are the window's spread on a shared box (slices
-2.8 % and listcopy +1.5 % in the same run) â neither row touches this path.

PEAK RSS DROPS: sortnum 79940 -> 60564 kB and sortstr 79688 -> 60472 kB
(-24 %), which is the adjustable vector and the copy-seq per sort going away.

=== SEMANTICS: 18 + 9 PROBE SHAPES vs perl 5.40.3 ===
scratch/s473v/probe/{sorts,misc-sort}.pl, compared with probecmp.pl against
perl AND a 2ac855aa extraction: NEW vs BASE **IDENTICAL** on every shape, and
vs perl the only difference is a WARNING line PCL does not emit
(`Argument "abc" isn't numeric in sort`), which is the #221 gap and
pre-existing.

Shapes covered: each kind ascending and descending (fixnums, doubles, mixed
reals, BIGNUMS, strings, a non-base character, `sort LIST` with no block),
mixed numbers-and-strings under BOTH comparators, one element, none, an undef
among numbers, two sources in one sort, a literal list, STABILITY, a sort
assigned back over its own source, a ref taken into the source before the
sort, a sort inside a sub, `keys`, `reverse sort`, sort-by-hash-value, a sort
of a `map` result, a NAMED sub comparator, a CODEREF comparator, and a NaN.

=== GUARD ===
Pl/t/classic-sort-01.t 29 -> 33 rows (every kind, the collection edges, and
the two aliasing shapes), including a PCL_OPT=none twin so the optimized
emission and the general form give the same answers.  These rows PASS on a
2ac855aa extraction, which is the right answer for a pure speed lever: they
are the correctness NET, the A/B is the bar.

=== WHAT WAS NOT DONE ===
The brief's (iii), ADOPTION â `p-array-adopt @x <fresh-sort-result>` as a
Kind-A emission, so the array assignment installs the fresh vector instead of
copying it.  Not attempted: it is an EMISSION change with its own licence
question (the producer's freshness) and its own probe list (a `\$x[0]` taken
before the assignment), and the three runtime levers above already took the
two rows past their 20 % bar and one of them past perl.  It stays available.
subject: The classic sort classifies its elements in ONE typed pass and sorts with a TYPED predicate (sortstr +148.7 %, 1.55x perl -> 0.70x; sortnum +78.6 %, 2.63x -> 1.58x; peak RSS 79.9 -> 60.6 MB)
